item.title: JPMorgan brings JPM Coin to Ethereum mainnet: what changes, and what it means for ETH
item.description:
JPMorgan Chase has extended JPM Coin (ticker JPMD), its US dollar deposit token, to the Ethereum mainnet. Approved institutional clients now have a second public network for moving dollars around the clock. Bloomberg reported the move on Monday, 19 October, citing the bank, and the Ethereum Foundation flagged it the same day. JPMD has run on Base, Coinbase’s Ethereum layer-2 network, since November 2025, and Base remains in service.

The move is a meaningful step for Ethereum as financial infrastructure. It is not, on current evidence, a new source of demand for ether. JPMD also remains closed to everyone except approved JPMorgan clients.

What JPM Coin actually is

JPMD is a deposit token: each unit represents one US dollar that a client holds at JPMorgan. That makes it different from a stablecoin such as USDC, which is issued by a non-bank company and backed by reserves held elsewhere. A deposit token is a claim on the bank itself. In effect, it is ordinary commercial bank money moved onto a blockchain.

The practical gain is timing. A transfer that would normally wait on banking hours and business-day settlement can complete almost instantly, at any hour, including weekends.

Why mainnet, when Base was cheaper

Base was promoted on sub-cent fees, and transactions on Ethereum mainnet typically cost more. So the move is not about saving money.

Kinexys, JPMorgan’s blockchain unit, said it chose Ethereum because so much liquidity and so many tokenized assets already sit there. That includes JPMorgan’s own products. The bank launched a tokenized money market fund on Ethereum in December 2025, seeded with $100 million of its own capital. With the cash token and the tokenized securities on the same network, a fund trade and its payment can settle together, without hopping between chains. The bank has also pointed to collateral and tokenized-asset settlement as uses, not just payments.

My read is that this is about settling where the assets already live. Fees are a secondary consideration.

What it does not mean for ETH

JPMD is not ether. Every mainnet transaction pays a fee in ETH, so more institutional activity adds to network usage at the margin. But JPMorgan has not disclosed how much JPMD exists on Ethereum, its contract address, which clients are using it, or how much activity it expects to move from Base.

Without those numbers, there is no basis for treating the launch as a buying catalyst for ETH. It is adoption of the network, not purchases of the coin. It also says nothing about whether JPMorgan holds ether.

What could change the interpretation

The deciding factor is volume. Kinexys is still a small part of a bank whose payments business moves roughly $12 trillion a day.

  • If the supply and activity become public and grow, the story shifts from symbolic to structural.
  • If mainnet usage stays thin, or most activity stays on Base, the launch looks more like positioning than a change in how JPMorgan moves money.

There is also a third venue. JPMorgan is separately working on a phased integration of JPM Coin with Canton Network, a privacy-focused blockchain built for financial markets. That plan was announced earlier this year and has no completed launch date. If activity shifts there, it would suggest the public mainnet is more of a showcase than the main route.

What to watch next

  • Usage data: any JPMorgan disclosure of JPMD supply or volume on mainnet, or a published contract address that lets readers track activity on-chain.
  • Settlement in practice: whether JPMD is used to settle the bank’s tokenized funds on Ethereum, which would confirm the logic behind the move.
  • Canton progress: any concrete launch date for the integration.
  • Rival banks: whether competitors move their deposit-token systems from private ledgers onto public networks.

Practical takeaway: for ETH investors, the useful signal will be usage, not the announcement. Wait for activity you can verify on-chain before treating this as a bullish development for ether. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BlackRock says French bond sell-off is a lesson in selectivity, upgrades US Treasuries
item.description:
BlackRock’s view reinforces a theme running through bank research this week: higher yields are now the norm, but the reasons behind them matter more than the level. For euro area bonds, the near-term focus is Moody’s decision on France’s credit rating, with a downgrade likely to pressure French debt and widen the gap over German Bunds. Any spillover selling in markets such as Spain could prove an opportunity if fundamentals hold up, in BlackRock’s view. Its upgrade of US Treasuries signals that the world’s largest asset manager sees value in longer-dated US debt at current yields, which could help cap further rises if other investors follow. A rising term premium driven by fiscal worries remains the main risk that could push yields higher still. Elevated energy costs linked to the Iran war add to inflation risks that feed into that premium.

---

Higher yields are everywhere, but BlackRock’s message is that not all of them are worth having, and France shows the difference between being paid more and being paid enough.

Summary:

  • BlackRock says the sharp sell-off in French government bonds shows why investors need to understand what is driving yields higher.
  • France’s 10-year yield has risen about 100 basis points since early August to nearly 5%, with a widening spread over German Bunds reflecting fiscal and political risk.
  • BlackRock sees today’s backdrop as materially different from the 2011-12 euro debt crisis, with stronger banks, more powerful ECB tools and euro area debt back at around 89% of GDP.
  • The firm upgraded US Treasuries last week, trimmed its underweight on Japanese government bonds and favours emerging market local-currency debt, especially in Latin America.
  • In corporate credit, it prefers higher-rated high-yield bonds and avoids both investment grade, under pressure from heavy AI-related issuance, and the weakest borrowers.
  • Markets are watching Moody’s decision on France’s credit rating and UK CPI data this week.

France’s government bond sell-off is a reminder that higher yields are not all equal, according to BlackRock, which says investors need to be increasingly selective as competition for capital intensifies.

BlackRock is the world’s largest asset manager and the owner of iShares, the biggest provider of exchange-traded funds. Its views are closely watched because changes in its asset allocation can influence flows across global markets, and its weekly research from the BlackRock Investment Institute is widely followed as a guide to how big institutional money is positioning.

In its latest commentary, BlackRock said rising government borrowing and AI-related investment are pushing up financing costs globally, exposing borrowers with weakening fundamentals to closer scrutiny. France’s 10-year yield has climbed about 100 basis points since early August to nearly 5%. Part of that reflects the broader global reset in interest rates, but BlackRock said the widening gap between French and German yields shows investors are also demanding extra compensation for France’s fiscal and political risks.

The firm sees risks of spillover from France but does not expect a repeat of the 2011-12 euro debt crisis. France’s government debt has risen from roughly 89% of GDP in 2011 to around 119% today, but the euro area’s overall debt ratio is back at about its 2011 level of around 89%. The region also has stronger banks and more powerful European Central Bank tools, though BlackRock noted intervention is not guaranteed. Indiscriminate selling could create opportunities in markets such as Spain, it said, but it remains neutral on euro area government bonds for now.

Higher yields are also creating opportunities. BlackRock said more than 80% of global bonds now yield above 4%, compared with about 6% five years ago. It upgraded US Treasuries last week, saying higher starting yields provide a bigger cushion against further rate increases and that markets may have priced in too much Federal Reserve tightening. It also trimmed its underweight on Japanese government bonds after long-term yields climbed above 3%, and favours emerging market local-currency debt, particularly in Latin America.

In corporate bonds, BlackRock favours higher-rated high-yield debt for income while avoiding both ends of the credit spectrum. Heavy AI-related issuance is weighing on investment-grade bonds, it said, while the weakest borrowers face tougher refinancing conditions.

The firm also pointed to last week’s tech sell-off, when concerns over the pace of AI spending pushed the Nasdaq down nearly 5%. It still favours AI within a neutral stance on US equities.

Attention now turns to Moody’s decision on France’s credit rating (due froday October 23) and to UK inflation data, which BlackRock will watch for a read on global price pressures. It sees a rise in the term premium, particularly if driven by fiscal concerns, as the key risk that could push yields higher.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump holds up Patriot missiles for Ukraine as Russian strikes intensify, officials say
item.description:
The dispute raises the risk of further escalation in a conflict that has increasingly targeted energy infrastructure on both sides, with the clearest risk for oil to the upside. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and diesel facilities have been a source of supply concern in product markets, and if Washington’s pressure on Kyiv to halt them fails, those attacks could intensify, tightening diesel supply further at a time when the Iran war is already keeping crude elevated. A weaker Ukrainian air defence could also leave its own energy system more exposed to Russian strikes. Against that, Friday’s US waiver of Russian oil and gas sanctions could ease some supply concerns if it allows more Russian barrels to reach buyers. On balance, the risk skew for oil, and especially diesel, leans higher while the conflict escalates.

--

As Russian missiles fall on Kyiv, the interceptors Ukraine needs to stop them are stuck awaiting Washington’s sign-off, and the US has not said why.

Summary:

  • The Trump administration has not approved the transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine, officials said on Monday, the Washington Post (gated) reported.
  • President Volodymyr Zelensky said the US is delaying Patriots that allies have already paid for under PURL, a NATO-coordinated purchasing mechanism, and that only part of the order has been approved.
  • Zelensky put US supply at about 12 interceptors a month, which he said is roughly a quarter of the rate under the previous administration; the US has not confirmed his figures.
  • Ukraine’s Patriot stocks are reported to be critically low or exhausted, as Russia launched ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv on consecutive nights.
  • Zelensky said he offered to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure in exchange for more missiles.
  • The US has not publicly explained the delay.

The Trump administration has not approved the transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles that Ukraine needs to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks, officials said on Monday, the Washington Post reported.

The newspaper said the delay comes as President Donald Trump has, in its words, embraced Russia and criticised Ukraine in recent weeks. The US government has not publicly explained the hold-up.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with Bloomberg at the weekend that the US is delaying Patriot missiles that allies have already paid for through PURL, a NATO-coordinated mechanism under which allied governments fund purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine. He said Washington had approved only part of the order and described the delay as not a technical issue. Zelensky said the US is now supplying about 12 interceptors a month, which he put at roughly a quarter of the rate under the previous administration. The US has not confirmed those figures.

The dispute comes as Ukraine’s air defences are under severe strain. Ukrainian officials and media reports have described Patriot stocks as critically low, with one report saying available missiles had been exhausted. Russia launched ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv on consecutive nights on 18 and 19 October.

Energy has become central to the tensions. Zelensky said he offered to stop Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure in exchange for more Patriot missiles, but that Washington wants the strikes to end without such a trade. The administration has threatened to restrict military and intelligence support unless Kyiv halts attacks on Russian oil refineries, according to reports.

The missile delay also follows Trump’s decision on Friday to sign an executive order waiving Russia-related sanctions and tariffs, including penalties on purchases of Russian oil and gas, that had been due to take effect under legislation he signed last month. Trump said the waiver served US national interests. Zelensky said the move would only help Russia.

For energy markets, the risk is further escalation. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have been a source of concern for diesel supply, and the loss of US support could leave Ukraine more exposed to attacks on its own infrastructure. With the Iran war already keeping crude prices elevated, any widening of the conflict’s energy front would add to upward pressure on oil, particularly diesel.

Attention now turns to whether Washington approves the outstanding missiles and whether Kyiv scales back its strikes on Russian energy facilities. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs sees $25 war risk premium in Brent, forecasts $90 in December and $80 in 2027
item.description:
Goldman’s estimate implies Brent is trading well above where supply and demand alone would put it, which leaves prices vulnerable to a sharp drop if the risk of escalation fades, and exposed to further spikes if the conflict widens. The forecast path points lower over time, with the bank expecting a shift into surplus from the fourth quarter to pull prices back toward $80 in 2027, a level consistent with UBS’s view that Brent will approach $80 next summer. Near-term support is likely to come from depleted inventories, including a US Strategic Petroleum Reserve at its lowest since 1982, and from investors using oil as a hedge for their stock and bond holdings. For inflation-sensitive markets, a fading premium would ease pressure on central banks and bond yields, while a renewed spike would reinforce the hawkish case.

---

Earlier:

  • US strategic oil reserve falls to lowest since 1982 as Iran war release drains stocks

---

Goldman Sachs reckons about $25 of every barrel of Brent is a bet on the Iran war getting worse, and if that bet does not pay off, the bank sees prices drifting back toward $80.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs estimates spot Brent carries a risk premium of nearly $25 a barrel above its fair value, reflecting the risk of supply curtailment and inventory draws if the Iran war escalates.
  • The bank raised its December 2026 Brent forecast to $90 a barrel from $85 and expects an average of $80 in 2027.
  • Persian Gulf exports have recovered to roughly their 2025 average since late September, including an estimated 4 million barrels a day of untracked shipments.
  • The global market was nearly balanced in September, with a deficit of 0.3 million barrels a day against 7.2 million in March, and Goldman expects a surplus from the fourth quarter.
  • Near-record-low inventories, restocking demand and oil’s use as a portfolio hedge continue to support prices.
  • Renewed escalation involving Iran or the Houthis that targets oil infrastructure is the main upside risk.

Goldman Sachs says Brent crude is carrying a risk premium of nearly $25 a barrel above its estimate of fair value, as markets price in the threat that the Iran war could escalate and disrupt supply again, even as Gulf exports recover.

In a research note published Friday, the bank raised its forecast for Brent in December 2026 to $90 a barrel from $85, while maintaining its view that prices will moderate to an average of $80 in 2027. Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research at Goldman Sachs, linked the premium to the possibility of further supply curtailment and inventory draws if the conflict intensifies.

The bank’s underlying picture of supply has improved markedly. Exports from the Persian Gulf have recovered to roughly their 2025 average since late September, Goldman said, including an estimated 4 million barrels a day of so-called dark exports, meaning shipments that move outside normal tracking. It expects Gulf supply to keep rising as exporters adapt and expand transport capacity, particularly pipelines and tanker fleets.

As a result, the global oil market has moved close to balance. Goldman estimates the deficit narrowed to 0.3 million barrels a day in September from 7.2 million in March, and it expects the market to move into surplus in the fourth quarter of 2026 and stay there through 2027. The bank describes that shift as the main driver of its expected price moderation.

Demand has also taken a significant hit. Goldman said consumption fell by 3.3 million barrels a day in the third quarter from a year earlier, mainly in China, the Middle East and OECD Asia. It expects most of that loss to be recovered by late 2027, although a lasting shift toward electric vehicles in China is likely to leave demand below its pre-shock path.

Several factors are keeping prices elevated in the meantime. Global inventories are near record lows, creating strong restocking demand, and investors have been buying oil as a hedge against moves in stocks and bonds. Emergency stocks have also been drawn down, with the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve falling last week to its lowest level since 1982.

Goldman sees the balance of risks to its forecasts tilted higher. A renewed escalation involving Iran or the Houthis that targets ports, pipelines or oil fields in the region would represent a significant upside risk to prices, the bank said.

Whether the premium fades will depend largely on the course of the conflict, with the pace of Gulf export recovery the key indicator to watch. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Explainer: China eyes overnight rate as main policy tool, what it means for markets
item.description:
The direct market effect is likely to be modest, because the PBOC is formalising a rate it already targets rather than cutting. The market read so far suggests limited impact, with China’s 30-year bond yield slipping only about 1 basis point and the overnight rate steady around 1.26%. The bigger question for traders is whether the new anchor is eventually set near today’s overnight level of about 1.25%, below the seven-day rate of 1.40%. Markets could treat that as a mild easing signal, which would tend to support Chinese bonds and weigh slightly on the yuan. For the Australian and New Zealand dollars, which often trade as proxies for China, the framework change matters less than whether it comes with genuine easing that lifts Chinese demand. Oil traders will watch the same thing, given China’s role as the world’s largest crude importer.

---

Separately, coming up later today:

  • China LPR preview: rates seen on hold for a 17th month after Q3 GDP beat

---

China’s central bank wants to steer its economy with the same short-term lever the Fed uses, and while that is not a rate cut, it changes which numbers traders need to watch.

Summary:

  • PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng said on Monday the central bank will study switching its main policy operations from a seven-day tenor to overnight, when the time is right.
  • The overnight reverse repo rate would replace the seven-day reverse repo rate, the main policy rate since 2024, as the central signal for monetary policy.
  • Pan said the overnight rate has effectively already become the PBOC’s target, and overnight deals make up more than 80% of interbank repo trading.
  • The change is not a rate cut, though the overnight rate sits near 1.25% compared with 1.40% for the seven-day rate.
  • Financially strong companies will be able to choose the overnight rate or the loan prime rate as a benchmark for floating-rate loans; households and small firms stay mainly on the LPR.
  • Traders will watch where the new rate is set, any knock-on for the yuan and bond yields, and whether it signals further easing.

China’s central bank is preparing to change the interest rate it uses to steer the economy. It is not a rate cut, but it changes how borrowing costs are set and which numbers traders need to watch.

What happened?

Speaking at the Financial Street Forum in Beijing on Monday, People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng said the central bank would study switching the main maturity of its open market operations from seven days to overnight when the time is right. That would make the overnight reverse repo rate the PBOC’s main policy rate.

What is a policy rate?

A policy rate is the single interest rate a central bank controls in order to influence all other borrowing costs in the economy. In the US, that role is played by the Federal Reserve’s federal funds rate, which is also an overnight rate.

A reverse repo is a short-term loan from the central bank to commercial banks, secured against bonds. By setting the rate on these loans, the PBOC influences what banks pay to borrow from each other, and that feeds through to the rates they charge customers.

What is changing?

Since 2024, the PBOC has used its seven-day reverse repo rate, currently 1.40%, as its main signal. Pan said the overnight interbank rate has effectively already become the central bank’s target, because it reflects short-term cash conditions closely and has become more stable.

Overnight deals make up more than 80% of repo trading between banks, so anchoring policy there would align the PBOC’s tool with where most of the market already operates, giving it more precise control. The central bank laid the groundwork in June, when it introduced overnight operations priced around the seven-day rate.

[Insert diagram: china-pboc-overnight-policy-rate-explainer.png]

Is this a rate cut?

No. The overnight repo rate is trading near 1.25%, below the seven-day rate, but the PBOC has said it will announce the operating rate for the new tool when the switch happens. The change is about how policy is delivered, not where it is set.

What happens to the loan prime rate?

The loan prime rate, or LPR, is the benchmark banks use to price most loans and mortgages. It currently follows the seven-day rate. Under the plan, financially strong companies will be able to agree with their banks to use either the overnight rate or the LPR as the benchmark for floating-rate loans. Loans to households and smaller firms will remain mainly tied to the LPR for now. The PBOC also plans to improve how LPR quotes are set, and to phase out the old system of benchmark deposit and lending rates.

What it means for traders

Chinese bonds: If the new rate is eventually set near today’s overnight level, markets may read it as a modest easing signal, which would tend to support government bonds. The initial reaction was small, with the 30-year yield slipping about 1 basis point.

The yuan: A lower policy anchor would narrow China’s interest rate advantage over other currencies, or widen its disadvantage, which could weigh on the yuan. Aligning with global practice may also help China’s push to make the yuan more widely used internationally.

Chinese stocks: A market-driven benchmark could lower borrowing costs for large, financially strong companies when rates fall, though it would also pass on rises more quickly. Banks may face some pressure on lending margins as loan pricing becomes more competitive.

Australian and New Zealand dollars: These currencies often trade as proxies for Chinese growth. For them, the framework change matters less than whether it comes alongside genuine stimulus that lifts China’s demand for commodities.

What to watch

  • The timing of the switch, which the PBOC has not set.
  • The operating rate for the new tool, and whether it lands below the current 1.40%.
  • Guidance on LPR reform, and on which companies can use the overnight benchmark.
  • Today’s loan prime rate fixing, due at 01:00 GMT, the last under the current system’s full grip.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS sees euro recovering to $1.16 by year-end, says slide to $1.11 overshoots fundamentals
item.description:
UBS’s view puts the euro’s recent weakness down mainly to sentiment rather than fundamentals, which would leave room for a rebound if French budget risks ease. The near removal of pricing for an October Fed hike takes away one of the dollar’s main supports, and UBS sees a sustained break below $1.10 as increasingly unlikely as a result. Energy is a key swing factor: the euro area is a large energy importer, so UBS’s expectation that Brent will approach $80 by next summer is supportive, while any escalation in the Iran war that lifts oil prices again would weigh on the currency. French bond spreads are the indicator to watch, since narrower spreads would back the recovery case and further widening would undercut it.

---

Earlier from analysts at the bank:

  • UBS says neocloud sell-off does not derail AI boom, favours hyperscalers and chipmakers

---

UBS thinks the market has sold the euro on worry rather than evidence, and with Fed hike bets fading and a French budget deal in sight, it sees the currency’s next move as up.

Summary:

  • UBS expects EUR/USD to recover to $1.16 by the end of 2026, after a slide from $1.17 to near $1.11 that it says has gone further than Europe’s economy justifies.
  • The bank blames stronger US data, concern over a possible US diesel export ban, rising global bond yields and worries over French public finances.
  • It does not expect a wider European debt crisis and sees a French budget deal as likely, possibly using Article 49.3.
  • With markets having almost fully priced out an October Fed hike, UBS sees a sustained fall below $1.10 as increasingly unlikely.
  • UBS likes buying the euro below $1.12, targeting $1.16, with an exit just below $1.10, and sees support at $1.10 and $1.08 and resistance at $1.13 and $1.17.
  • Its forecasts rise to $1.18 in March 2027 and $1.20 by mid-2027, after the French presidential election.

UBS expects the euro to recover to $1.16 against the dollar by the end of 2026, arguing that its recent slide toward $1.11 has gone further than Europe’s economic fundamentals justify and that markets have turned too pessimistic on the region.

Strategists at the bank’s Chief Investment Office said the euro’s fall from $1.17 reflected a combination of stronger US economic data, concern about a possible US ban on diesel exports, rising global bond yields and worries over French public finances. The euro was trading around $1.12 when the report was published.

France has been a particular source of pressure, with the gap between French and German government bond yields widening significantly in recent weeks. UBS does not expect a broader European debt crisis, however, and sees a French budget agreement as likely. That could come through Article 49.3 of the French constitution, which allows the government to pass legislation without a parliamentary vote, at the risk of facing a no-confidence motion. A deal should help narrow spreads and support the euro, the bank said.

On the US side, UBS noted that stronger-than-expected inflation data initially pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher, but the move reversed, with yields falling back and the dollar ending the day weaker. Markets have now almost entirely priced out a US rate hike in October, which UBS said makes a sustained drop below $1.10 increasingly unlikely.

The bank said it favours buying the euro below $1.12, targeting $1.16, with an exit point just below $1.10 to limit losses. It also sees value in selling downside protection in the currency pair to earn yield, given the rise in volatility. UBS identified support at $1.10 and $1.08, with resistance at $1.13 and then at August’s highs around $1.17.

Further out, UBS expects the euro to reach $1.18 by March 2027 and $1.20 by June and September 2027, after France’s presidential election in April and May. The bank also expects energy prices to ease next year, with Brent crude approaching $80 a barrel by the summer.

UBS flagged the US midterm elections as a risk not reflected in market pricing, saying a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would likely be a modest negative for the dollar, though mainly a 2027 story, since the new Congress takes office in January.

The main risks to its view are further strong US data, a material deterioration in European growth or a significant escalation in French fiscal concerns. Softer US data, easing geopolitical tensions, lower energy prices and a steadier outlook for France could speed up the recovery.  

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS says neocloud sell-off does not derail AI boom, favours hyperscalers and chipmakers
item.description:
The UBS view separates two trades that moved together last week: highly leveraged neoclouds, whose models depend on cheap funding, and cash-rich hyperscalers and chipmakers, whose earnings continue to grow. If that distinction takes hold, it could support a rotation within tech rather than a broad exit, with semiconductor names and the large cloud platforms holding up better than specialist GPU renters. The rates backdrop is the key swing factor. With bond yields elevated across developed markets, any further rise in funding costs would weigh most on the neocloud segment. Hyperscaler results over the coming weeks will be the next test, with UBS expecting cloud revenue growth to accelerate.

---

The UBS note was before the bounce on Monday, kudos to them!

  • investingLive Americas market news wrap: AI trades rebound but so does oil

---

Specialist AI cloud firms are feeling the squeeze from higher rates, but UBS argues that is a funding problem for one corner of the market rather than a crack in AI demand itself.

Summary:

  • Shares of neoclouds, specialist providers that rent out AI computing capacity, came under heavy pressure last week on concerns about their growth models as rates stay higher for longer.
  • The sell-off helped drive a weekly fall of about 4.5% in the Nasdaq, its biggest weekly loss since June, with competition from China and revenue worries at AI labs adding to the pressure.
  • UBS says the weakness does not undermine the broader AI investment cycle and expects AI capex to rise 33% to $1.2 trillion in 2027, with neoclouds under 10% of that spending.
  • GPU rental prices continue to rise: rates for four-year-old chips are up nearly 30% this year, and for two-year-old chips about 35%.
  • UBS says strong results from TSMC and ASML support the view that AI demand remains robust.
  • The bank limits exposure to neoclouds and favours well-funded hyperscalers, quality chip and hardware names, and defensive areas of tech.

UBS says last week’s sharp sell-off in so-called neocloud stocks reflects funding and execution risks in one corner of the AI market rather than a weakening in demand for artificial intelligence, and the bank remains positive on the sector’s structural growth.

Neoclouds are specialist providers that rent out graphics processing unit (GPU) computing power for AI workloads. Their shares came under intense pressure last week as investors questioned their business models against a backdrop of higher-for-longer interest rates. Competitive threats from China and concerns over revenue growth at leading AI developers added to the selling, which helped push the Nasdaq down about 4.5% for the week, its steepest weekly decline since June.

UBS argues the distinction between neoclouds and the large hyperscale cloud providers is central. Neoclouds typically offer a single product and must invest heavily upfront before contracted revenue turns into cash flow, which leaves them exposed to rising funding costs. Hyperscalers are also borrowing more to finance their AI buildout, but their broad cloud platforms generate diversified revenue. UBS estimates their cost of debt at a manageable 6.5% to 7%, against returns on new data centre investment of around 25% or more.

The bank expects the overall impact on AI spending to be limited while computing capacity remains scarce. It forecasts AI capital expenditure rising 33% to $1.2 trillion in 2027, with neoclouds accounting for less than a tenth of that. A further sharp rise in funding costs could still hit the neocloud segment, UBS said, though strong customer credit quality and large advance orders should provide some protection.

Rental prices offer one of the clearest signals. UBS said rates for four-year-old GPUs rose 7% over the past month, taking their gain this year to nearly 30%, while rates for two-year-old GPUs are up 35% year to date. Rising prices for older hardware point to demand still outstripping supply.

Third-quarter results support that view. UBS noted that TSMC said demand remains strong and expects its capital spending over 2026 to 2028 to be meaningfully higher than in the previous three years, while ASML reported strong order intake for 2028, with interest stretching into 2030. UBS also expects hyperscalers to report accelerating cloud revenue growth.

The bank acknowledged that funding and execution risks could feed on each other, with tighter credit slowing deployment and delays postponing the cash needed to service debt. It recommends a selective approach: limiting exposure to neoclouds, favouring well-funded hyperscalers and high-quality semiconductor and hardware names, and considering defensive tech areas such as payment networks, select consumer electronics and select software. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US strategic oil reserve falls to lowest since 1982 as Iran war release drains stocks
item.description:
A smaller emergency reserve reduces Washington’s ability to respond to any fresh supply shock, which could add to the risk premium in crude if the Iran war escalates. Goldman Sachs estimated last week that spot Brent carries a premium of nearly $25 a barrel above fair value (I'll have more to come on this separately), citing near-record-low global inventories as one of the factors keeping prices high. Because the release is structured as an exchange, around 200 million barrels are due to be returned to the reserve, so refilling will add a source of demand later and could support prices further out. For now, continued drawdowns add barrels to the market at a time of tight supply, but traders are likely to watch how much firepower remains in reserve.

---

Earlier:

  • investingLive Americas market news wrap: AI trades rebound but so does oil

---

America’s emergency oil stockpile has been doing exactly what it was built for, and the cost is a reserve now back at levels not seen since the early 1980s.

Summary:

  • Crude stocks in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to around 283 million barrels last week, the lowest since October 1982, Reuters reported, citing Department of Energy data.
  • The drawdowns are part of a US commitment to release 172 million barrels, announced on 11 March.
  • The US release is part of a 400 million barrel coordinated release agreed by 32 IEA member countries in response to Middle East supply disruptions.
  • The release is structured as an exchange, with around 200 million barrels due to be returned to the reserve.
  • The SPR is less than 40% full, against an authorised capacity of 714 million barrels across four Gulf Coast sites.

Crude oil stocks in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to around 283 million barrels last week, their lowest level since October 1982, Reuters reported, citing data from the Department of Energy.

The decline reflects an ongoing release of 172 million barrels from the reserve, which the US agreed to on 11 March as part of a coordinated response to supply disruptions caused by the war with Iran. The US contribution forms the largest share of a 400 million barrel release of crude oil and refined products agreed unanimously by the 32 member countries of the International Energy Agency.

The release has been slower than first planned. The Department of Energy said in March that deliveries would take about 120 days at planned discharge rates, which implied completion by around mid-July. Instead, drawdowns have continued into October. Based on Energy Information Administration data, the reserve now holds roughly 130 million barrels less than when the release began.

The reserve was created in the 1970s, after the Arab oil embargo exposed how vulnerable the US was to supply shocks. It has an authorised storage capacity of 714 million barrels held in underground salt caverns at four sites along the Gulf Coast. At current levels, it is less than 40% full.

Unlike an outright sale, the release is structured as an exchange. Companies that take barrels from the reserve are required to return them later with additional volumes, and the Department of Energy has said it expects to recover around 200 million barrels within a year at no cost to taxpayers. That means the drawdown should eventually reverse, although refilling will itself add to demand in the oil market once it begins.

The low level comes as crude prices remain elevated. Goldman Sachs said last week that spot Brent carries a risk premium of nearly $25 a barrel above its estimate of fair value, pointing to the threat of further supply disruption and near-record-low global inventories. A depleted emergency reserve leaves the US with less room to respond if the conflict escalates and supply is disrupted again.

The pace of further drawdowns, and the timing of any refill, will be closely watched by oil traders in the coming months.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs estimates central banks bought 79 tonnes of gold in August, led by China
item.description:
Steady central bank buying gives gold a source of demand that tends to be less sensitive to price than investment flows, which can help cushion pullbacks driven by speculative or ETF selling. That matters more now that bond yields are high across developed markets, a backdrop that would normally weigh on a non-yielding asset like gold. The pick-up in August suggests official buyers have not been deterred by elevated prices. For China, buying well above its reported additions would point to a continued push to diversify reserves away from the dollar. Geopolitical risk, including the Iran war, remains a parallel driver of safe-haven demand and could reinforce the official-sector bid.

---

Earlier from GS:

  • Goldman Sachs says rising global bond yields reflect a growing competition for capital

---

Central banks are still buying gold at several times their old pace, and Goldman Sachs sees that steady official demand as a floor under the market rather than a passing phase.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs estimates central banks bought 79 tonnes of gold in August, Reuters reported.
  • That is well above the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes a month.
  • China was the largest identifiable buyer, with an estimated 25 tonnes.
  • Goldman says it continues to see central bank demand as a structural support for gold.
  • The August estimate is a sharp step up from Goldman’s estimate of 44 tonnes for July.
  • Goldman’s estimate for China exceeds the roughly 20 tonnes the PBOC officially reported for August.

Central banks bought an estimated 79 tonnes of gold in August, well above their long-run pace, according to Goldman Sachs in a note Monday, which said official sector demand remains a structural support for the metal.

The bank said August purchases were far higher than the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes a month, putting buying at more than four times that historical rate. China was the largest identifiable buyer during the month, with Goldman estimating its purchases at 25 tonnes.

The August figure marks a sharp acceleration from Goldman’s previous monthly estimate of 44 tonnes for July, suggesting that central banks continued to add to reserves even with gold prices elevated.

Goldman’s figures are estimates rather than official totals. The bank builds its monthly gauge from trade and flow data instead of relying only on central bank disclosures, which tend to arrive with a delay and do not capture every purchase. As a result, its numbers often run above reported figures and can be revised as more data become available.

The gap is visible in China’s case. The People’s Bank of China officially reported adding around 20 tonnes of gold in August, extending a buying streak that has run for nearly two years. Goldman’s estimate of 25 tonnes suggests China’s actual accumulation was larger than disclosed, consistent with the bank’s earlier findings that Chinese purchases have run above official numbers this year.

The scale of buying since 2022 reflects a broader shift in reserve management. Many central banks, particularly in emerging markets, have been increasing gold holdings to diversify away from the US dollar and reduce exposure to financial sanctions, a trend that accelerated after Western countries froze Russian reserves following the invasion of Ukraine.

For the gold market, the significance lies in the nature of that demand. Central banks tend to buy steadily and with less sensitivity to price than investors, which can provide support during periods when speculative positioning or ETF holdings are being reduced. Goldman’s view is that this official-sector bid is a lasting feature of the market rather than a temporary one.

Official data already point to continued buying, with the PBOC reporting its largest monthly addition in about three years in September, its 23rd straight month of purchases. October’s figures, due around 7 November, will show whether that pace has held.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bank of Canada preview: Scotiabank expects a 25 bp hike next week despite softer core CPI
item.description:
With markets pricing about 18 basis points of tightening, a hike next week is the base case but not fully locked in, leaving room for the Canadian dollar and front-end yields to move on the decision and guidance. Canada’s two-year bonds have been the weakest front end among the major markets, reflecting that shift in pricing. Oil is central to the outlook: Scotiabank flags the risk of an escalation in the Iran war after the US midterms, which could push energy and commodity prices higher and add to Canadian inflation pressure. Higher crude would normally support the Canadian dollar, but it would also strengthen the case for further tightening. If the Bank of Canada holds instead, the loonie would likely weaken, and markets could read the pause as a signal that policymakers are prepared to tolerate inflation near the top of the target range.

-

September’s inflation report gave the Bank of Canada a softer headline to point to, but Scotiabank argues that summer travel coming off is no reason to hold rates while the forward-looking risks keep building.

Summary:

  • Scotiabank expects the Bank of Canada to raise rates by 25 basis points at its meeting next Wednesday, 28 October.
  • Markets were pricing about 18 basis points of tightening after September CPI, unchanged from levels set after Governor Tiff Macklem’s weekend remarks.
  • Headline CPI rose to 3.1% y/y in September, a tick below forecasts and at the top of the bank’s 1% to 3% target range.
  • Core measures eased in September, but the bank says a sharp drop in travel prices was the main drag and smoothed trends remain warm.
  • Scotiabank sees a hike as insurance against upside inflation risks, including possible Iran war escalation, higher commodity prices and fiscal expansion.
  • Business and consumer surveys and an Alberta vote are still to come before the decision.

Scotiabank expects the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates by a quarter point at its meeting next Wednesday, arguing that underlying inflation remains warm enough to justify an insurance hike even after a softer-than-expected September price report.

Consumer prices rose 3.1% from a year earlier in September, up from 3.0% in August but a tick below forecasts. That leaves headline inflation at the top end of the central bank’s 1% to 3% target range. Core measures eased in the month, but Scotiabank said upward revisions to earlier data and the smoothed trend still point to persistent pressure, with its preferred three-month averages of the central bank’s core measures running at around 2.6% to 2.7% on an annualised basis. 

The bank attributed much of September’s softness to a sharp drop in travel prices as the summer holiday season ended. Travel services prices fell by roughly a quarter on an annualised basis, and car rental prices by close to 40%, a fall far larger than the usual seasonal pattern. Scotiabank said such moves warrant caution over data quality and argued that a slump in travel spending is not a reason to keep rates on hold. Excluding travel, it said core inflation would have been firmer and more broadly based, with almost 60% of the CPI basket rising by 2% or more from a year earlier.

Scotiabank also pointed to a shift in tone from Governor Tiff Macklem, who it says has turned his attention toward forward-looking inflation risks rather than backward-looking data. The central bank dropped its description of the policy rate as appropriate at its previous meeting, which Scotiabank reads as a warning. The bank said policy sits at the lower bound of neutral and is negative in real terms, and that the central bank’s staff have historically tended to underestimate inflation at turning points.

Markets appear to share the view. Pricing for next week held at about 18 basis points of tightening after the CPI release, and Canada’s two-year bonds remain the weakest-performing front end among major markets. Scotiabank said that with a hike largely priced, failing to deliver would loosen financial conditions in a way that would be hard to justify.

Looking further ahead, the bank flagged the risk of an escalation in the Iran war after the US midterm elections, higher energy and commodity prices, and another expansionary federal budget. It argued monetary policy needs to offset some of those pressures as spare capacity closes. Business and consumer surveys from the central bank, along with a vote in Alberta, are still due before the decision.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morgan Stanley IM says bond yields are rising for the right reasons, favours US and Japan
item.description:
Morgan Stanley IM’s view offers a more benign reading of the yield rise than fears of fiscal strain or a growth scare, and if markets adopt it, US equities could keep absorbing higher yields as long as earnings deliver. The house’s underweight in duration and preference for credit suggest it expects long-dated Treasuries to stay under pressure rather than rally. Its tilt toward Japan aligns with strong nominal growth there, while the underweight on Europe points to relative weakness in European stocks. For oil, the inflation component of high nominal growth is worth watching, since energy costs tied to the Iran war feed directly into it. The main risk to the thesis is a disappointing Q3 earnings season, which would remove the cushion Caron says is supporting equity prices.

---

Earlier:

  • Goldman Sachs says rising global bond yields reflect a growing competition for capital

---

Morgan Stanley’s investment arm reads the rise in Treasury yields as a sign that the US economy is running hot, and it is betting US earnings can stay one step ahead of borrowing costs.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley Investment Management, which oversees around $2 trillion, favours US and Japanese equities and is underweight Europe.
  • Jim Caron, CIO of its Portfolio Solutions Group, says higher yields reflect resilient nominal growth rather than economic stress, with US real growth plus inflation running at about 6.5%.
  • The US 10-year yield peaked at around 5.3% on 5 October this year before easing to around 5.1%.
  • The firm is underweight duration and overweight credit, and has cut interest rate sensitivity across its portfolios.
  • Caron said potential Democratic gains in November’s midterms could narrow US opportunities toward large, established companies such as AI hyperscalers.
  • He said private credit has moved past its correction phase, with more exits allowing capital to be deployed at today’s higher rates.

Morgan Stanley Investment Management says the rise in government bond yields this year reflects strong economic growth rather than stress, and is not yet a warning sign for equities, as it maintains a preference for US and Japanese stocks over those in Europe.

Jim Caron, chief investment officer of the Portfolio Solutions Group at the firm, which managed around $2 trillion in assets at the end of September, told journalists in a recent webinar that higher yields increasingly reflect resilient nominal growth. Nominal growth combines real economic expansion with inflation, and Caron put that figure at about 6.5% in the US. He pointed to firm growth, robust labour markets and productivity gains as factors supporting activity while helping to ease inflation pressure.

The US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to around 5.3% on 5 October, its high for the year, before easing to around 5.1%. Caron said such a move was natural given the pace of nominal growth, arguing that bonds are not signalling a slowdown and that yields are rising for sound reasons. In his view, bonds have taken a knock but are not broken.

The question for investors is when higher yields begin to weigh seriously on stocks. Caron’s answer rests on earnings. He said strong nominal growth points to healthy corporate cash generation and described expectations for third-quarter earnings as very robust. He argued that the US equity market is better placed than any other to benefit from that growth, and said Japan is also well positioned after a period of strong nominal growth.

That view offers a different explanation for the same trend highlighted by Goldman Sachs (link to post above), which has attributed the global rise in yields to intensifying competition for capital from government borrowing and AI investment. Both see higher yields as the new backdrop; they differ on whether it is driven mainly by demand for funding or by the strength of the economy itself.

In bonds, Morgan Stanley IM is underweight duration, overweight credit and has reduced interest rate sensitivity across its portfolios. On politics, Caron said potential Democratic gains in November’s midterm elections, and any pushback against the administration’s deregulation agenda, could narrow US opportunities and favour large, established firms such as AI hyperscalers.

On private markets, Caron said private credit has completed its correction phase after stress earlier this year in areas such as software. A pick-up in exits is creating room to deploy capital at today’s higher rates, he said, though he expects the next phase to be slower.

The third-quarter earnings season will be a key test of whether profits can continue to outpace the rise in borrowing costs.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs says rising global bond yields reflect a growing competition for capital
item.description:
If Goldman is right that higher yields reflect structural demand for capital rather than a temporary inflation scare, the pressure on long-dated bonds may prove persistent, keeping term premiums elevated across developed markets. For equities, the read-through is that index-level strength is resting heavily on earnings, so any disappointment from AI-linked leaders could expose valuations that have already compressed. Rising Japanese yields matter beyond Japan, since higher returns at home can draw domestic investors back from overseas markets and support the yen. Australian and UK bonds, already above 5%, stand out as the high-yield end of the developed world, which may support the Australian dollar and sterling on carry grounds. Higher government borrowing tied to energy security also links the bond story to oil, as elevated energy costs feed both fiscal needs and inflation risk.

---

Earlier:

  • Nasdaq and S&P rebounds; Dow slips

---

Governments and AI builders are both lining up for funding, and Goldman Sachs argues that higher yields are simply the price investors are now charging to stand in that queue.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says higher government bond yields have become the global norm, with 10-year yields up in every major developed market this year.
  • Since January, 10-year yields have risen by around 100 bps in Japan, about 85 bps in the US and close to 80 bps in both the euro area and the UK.
  • UK and Australian 10-year yields are above 5%, while Japan’s is near 3% after years below zero.
  • The bank attributes the rise to intensifying competition for capital, as governments borrow for defence, energy security and infrastructure and companies raise record sums for AI infrastructure and data centres.
  • Goldman says choosing well now matters as much as market exposure, with bonds once again a real source of return but not always a reliable hedge for stocks.
  • The bank says S&P 500 forward valuations have slipped toward April’s lows even as the index sits near record highs, with strong earnings, especially in AI-linked names, masking the pressure.

Goldman Sachs says higher bond yields have become the global norm, arguing that a growing competition for capital, rather than a passing shock, explains why borrowing costs have climbed across every major developed market this year.

In a note, the bank highlighted the breadth of the move. Since January, the 10-year government bond yield has risen by around 100 basis points in Japan, about 85 basis points in the US and close to 80 basis points in both the euro area and the UK. Goldman said five of the six markets it tracks recorded their highest monthly average yield since at least 2019 in September. UK and Australian 10-year yields are now above 5%, while Japan’s is approaching 3%, a striking shift for a market where yields sat below zero for years.

The bank’s explanation centres on demand for funding. Many governments are borrowing more to pay for defence, energy security and infrastructure, while companies are raising record amounts to build AI infrastructure and data centres. Goldman said these combined needs are pushing up demand for capital, and investors are asking for greater compensation to lend. In the bank’s framing, higher yields are what that competition looks like in practice.

That environment, Goldman argues, rewards discrimination over broad exposure. The bank describes selectivity as the new source of excess return, saying that choosing well now matters as much as simply being invested. Higher starting yields have restored bonds as a genuine source of return, Goldman said, although they may not always offer a dependable hedge when stocks fall. Among equities, the bank sees companies that can fund their own growth, or that earn more than their cost of capital, as potentially better positioned.

Goldman also pointed to what it sees as rational behaviour in equity valuations. The forward multiple on the S&P 500 has drifted back toward the lows seen in April, even as the index trades near record highs. In the bank’s view, strong earnings growth, particularly among AI-linked companies, may be masking the valuation pressure that higher yields would otherwise put on share prices.

The implication is that equity strength is increasingly dependent on earnings delivery. If yields stay elevated and profit growth slows, the cushion that has protected headline index levels could thin, leaving investors more exposed to the gap between rising financing costs and corporate returns. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq and S&P rebounds; Dow slips
item.description:
U.S. stocks closed mixed to start the new trading week, with the Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 gaining more than 1% while the Dow industrial average edged lower.

After last week’s selling, buyers returned to some of the technology names. Amazon led the large-cap rebound with a gain of nearly 5%, while storage, semiconductor and software shares featured prominently among the strongest performers.

However, the gains were far from universal. More stocks declined than advanced on both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. Buyers are making a play, but broader participation would give the recovery more credibility.

The closing numbers

  • Dow Industrial Average: fell 35.81 points, or 0.07%, to 51,966.60.

  • S&P 500: rose 33.20 points, or 0.43%, to 7,692.64.

  • Nasdaq Composite: rose 290.85 points, or 1.11%, to 26,430.89.

  • Russell 2000: rose 6.92 points, or 0.25%, to 2,728.29.

  • Nasdaq 100: rose 341.80 points, or 1.17%, to 29,529.35.

Amazon leads, with help from chips and software

Amazon was the standout among the major technology names, rising 4.98% to $262.45. Nvidia added 1.38% to $217.09, while Microsoft gained 0.84% to $533.52.

Apple did not join the advance, slipping 0.15% to $342.94. That divergence is another reminder that even within the largest technology companies, traders are picking their spots.

Some of the stronger individual performers included:

  • Western Digital: +6.12%.

  • SanDisk: +5.50%.

  • Datadog: +5.35%.

  • SK Hynix ADR: +4.67%.

  • Palantir: +4.36%.

  • Marvell: +4.06%.

The buying extended beyond technology. Celsius gained 5.43%, while Moderna rose 4.07%.

Dow weakness reflects a divided market

The Dow finished modestly lower, with 19 components declining and 11 advancing.

Amazon’s strong gain, together with advances in IBM (+1.85%), Nvidia (+1.38%) and UnitedHealth (+1.36%), helped cushion the downside. However, several financial, healthcare and other Dow components moved lower:

  • JPMorgan: −1.79%.

  • Amgen: −1.75%.

  • 3M: −1.66%.

  • Merck: −1.58%.

  • Verizon: −1.44%.

The result was a session where the technology-heavy indices delivered solid gains, but the average stock had a more difficult day.

Market breadth leaves buyers with work to do

The underlying participation figures were less encouraging than the headline index gains:

  • S&P 500: 166 stocks advanced versus 318 that declined.

  • Nasdaq: 1,432 advanced versus 1,768 that declined.

  • Nasdaq 100: 60 advanced versus 40 that declined.

  • NYSE: 611 advanced versus 1,181 that declined.

The Nasdaq 100 had better participation within its own group. Across the broader market, however, decliners held the advantage.

That does not erase the gains. It does tell traders that Monday’s rebound was concentrated. The next step for buyers is to hold those gains and bring more stocks along.

The trading lesson: look beneath the index

An index can rise even when more of its stocks fall. In a market-cap-weighted index such as the S&P 500, larger companies carry more influence. Strong gains in a handful of heavyweights can outweigh smaller declines across many other stocks.

For traders, the index provides the broader backdrop, but each stock still needs its own technical roadmap. A rising Nasdaq can help sentiment. Your stock still needs to get above—and stay above—its resistance levels.

Monday gave buyers some breathing room. Whether they can build on it is the next test.

item.title: NZDUSD buyers build momentum as the recovery approaches its next resistance test
item.description:
Buyers start to turn the technical picture around

The NZDUSD buyers have started to turn the shorter-term technical picture around after the prolonged move lower. The recovery has come in steps, with each break giving buyers a little more confidence. However, there is still work to do before the recent gains can develop into a more meaningful correction of the broader decline.

Thursday’s moving average break provided the catalyst

The first step came on Thursday when the price moved away from the 100- and 200-hour moving averages (blue and green lines on the chart above). Those moving averages help define the shorter-term bias and give traders a reference for risk. When the price can move above both and build distance from them, it suggests sellers are losing some control and buyers are becoming more willing to step in.

That move provided the catalyst. Friday’s break above the swing area between 0.56225 and 0.5633 provided the next piece of technical evidence (see lower yellow area on the chart above). 

Friday’s breakout gave buyers more confidence

Why does that matter? Swing areas identify levels where buyers and sellers have previously made decisions. When the price moves above a former ceiling, it forces traders to reassess. Sellers leaning against that resistance lose some of their technical protection, while buyers gain a level they can use to define risk on a pullback.

The break above 0.56225–0.5633 therefore strengthened the bullish shift and opened the door for the recovery to extend toward the next resistance zone between 0.5673 and 0.5686.

The next hurdle: 0.5673–0.5686

Several swing levels formed in that region during September before sellers pushed the price lower. As the price returns, traders will be watching to see whether sellers defend the area again or whether buyers can generate enough momentum to push through it.

For buyers, getting above the zone is one step. Staying above it is what would give the break more credibility. A brief move above resistance followed by a quick reversal would leave the market vulnerable to another rotation lower. Buyers would have had their shot, and a failure to hold the break would suggest sellers are still prepared to defend the broader downtrend.

A break higher targets the 38.2% retracement

A sustained move above 0.5686 would clear another obstacle and put the 38.2% retracement of the decline from the August high at 0.57258 in play.

That retracement is an important benchmark for judging the strength of the recovery. Buyers can make progress on the hourly chart while the broader move remains corrective. Reaching and eventually breaking the 38.2% level would add evidence that they are taking back more control. Until then, the recovery still has something to prove.

Former resistance becomes the support to watch

On the downside, the 0.56225–0.5633 swing area becomes the support zone to watch. The former ceiling now gives buyers an opportunity to show they can defend the breakout.

Holding above that area on a pullback would keep the recovery structure intact and give buyers a foundation for another push higher. A move back below it would weaken the breakout story and bring the hourly moving averages back into focus.

Follow the technical steps and define the risk

That is the value of following the technical steps. Each break creates a new target, but it also creates a reference for risk. Traders can judge the recovery by whether the price continues to clear resistance and then holds those levels as support.

The buyers have made progress. They moved away from the hourly moving averages and cleared the first swing area. Getting through 0.5673–0.5686—and staying above it—is the next test of their strength.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: China LPR preview: rates seen on hold for a 17th month after Q3 GDP beat
item.description:
A hold is widely expected and should be largely priced, so any reaction is likely to come only from a surprise. An unexpected cut (not gonna happen ... thats how unespected it'd be!) would probably weigh on the yuan, given the already wide gap between US and Chinese yields, while giving Chinese equities and property names a lift. The Australian and New Zealand dollars, often traded as proxies for Chinese growth, could firm on a cut as a sign of extra support for demand. For oil, any easing from the world’s largest crude importer would be a modest positive for demand, at a time when Iran war disruptions are already keeping supply risk elevated. A hold keeps the focus on liquidity tools such as a reserve requirement ratio cut as the more likely form of any future easing.

---

With growth back inside Beijing’s target range and the Fed tightening, the PBOC has little reason to move its lending benchmarks and good reason to keep its powder dry.

Summary:

  • China’s monthly loan prime rate fixing is due on Tuesday, with the one-year LPR expected to stay at 3.0% and the five-year at 3.5%.
  • A hold would make it the 17th straight month without a change; both tenors were last cut in May 2025.
  • The LPR is compiled from submissions by 20 designated banks; the one-year rate underpins most loans and the five-year rate guides mortgage pricing.
  • The LPRs take their cue from the PBOC’s seven-day reverse repo rate, its main policy rate since a mid-2024 framework change.
  • Monday’s data showed Q3 GDP growth of 4.5%, above forecasts, with retail sales and industrial output also beating expectations.
  • A Reuters poll sees the LPRs and the reserve requirement ratio unchanged through the first quarter of 2027.

China is expected to leave its benchmark lending rates unchanged at Tuesday’s monthly fixing, which would extend the hold to a 17th consecutive month, after stronger-than-expected third-quarter growth eased pressure on Beijing to add monetary support. The one-year loan prime rate is seen staying at 3.0% and the five-year LPR at 3.5%, with the fixing due at 9:00 a.m. Beijing time (0100 GMT / 2100 US Eastern time).

The loan prime rate is China’s benchmark for domestic lending and the reference point for pricing new bank loans. It is compiled each month from rate submissions by a panel of 20 designated commercial banks, although the People’s Bank of China retains strong influence over the outcome. There are two tenors: the one-year LPR, on which most new and outstanding loans are based, and the five-year LPR, which serves as the reference for mortgage pricing. The LPR replaced China’s old benchmark lending rate in August 2019 as part of a shift toward more market-based rate setting.

In practice, the LPR follows the central bank’s lead. Since a framework change in mid-2024, the PBOC has treated its seven-day reverse repo rate as its main policy rate, replacing the medium-term lending facility rate that previously served as the anchor for banks’ submissions. When the seven-day rate moves, the LPRs typically follow, and with it unchanged, the benchmarks have stayed put. Both tenors were last cut in May 2025, by 10 basis points each, following a larger quarter-point reduction in October 2024.

Monday’s data strengthened the case for patience. Gross domestic product grew 4.5% from a year earlier in the third quarter, slightly ahead of forecasts and up from 4.3% in the second quarter, lifting growth back to the bottom of Beijing’s 4.5% to 5% target range. September retail sales and industrial output also beat expectations, though property investment fell by around 21% in the first nine months of the year, underlining the weakness in housing. A Reuters poll conducted ahead of the release found economists expect the LPRs and the reserve requirement ratio to remain unchanged through the first quarter of 2027.

External conditions also argue against a cut. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September and signalled more could follow, widening the policy gap with China, and the premium on 10-year US Treasuries over Chinese government bonds was near a record high last month. Further easing would risk adding pressure on the yuan. At home, policymakers face weak credit demand and squeezed bank margins, which limit the appeal of lower lending rates.

A hold would keep attention on fourth-quarter data and on whether Beijing leans on liquidity measures or fiscal support rather than rate cuts if growth falters again.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump approval falls to record low. Poll shows Republicans losing badly in midterms

  • That 12-point advantage is the largest of the current election cycle, according to Reuters/Ipsos.

The generic ballot doesn’t translate directly into seats but that is an uncomfortable gap for Republicans. If it carries through to election day, it points to an acrimonious final two years for Trump in the White House, including investigations on Epstein, the Iran war and corruption.

For markets, it's likely that Democrat control of the House has been priced in for some time but a complete rout could kick off a broader repudation of Trump, even by his own party. That could strengthen the agenda for peace in the Middle East and an end to the trade war. At the same time, Trump under constant investigations could make him more impulsive and combative.

There is also the question of how Trump responds to deteriorating polling and how he wants to manage his legacy. Does it encourage a more conciliatory approach aimed at delivering economic wins, or a harder push on his least-popular policies? Will he want to be remembered as the President that started an endless war with Iran?

I would be careful about treating this as an immediate dollar or equity-market signal. The more useful takeaway is that the risk of a constrained White House is becoming harder to ignore and we count down to the vote.

The poll was taken over four days ending today.

item.title: USDJPY buyers land the punches, but sellers are still standing
item.description:
Sellers have repeatedly defended the ceiling

The USDJPY technical story since September 23 has centered on two key levels: the 50% midpoint of the decline from the July 2026 high to the September low at 158.419, and the 200-day moving average, currently at 158.565.

The midpoint has remained fixed, while the 200-day moving average (higher green line) has edged higher from around 158.42. Together, they have created a resistance area where sellers have repeatedly leaned against the market and pushed the price lower.

There have been at least 10 tests of that area, with three separate breaks above both technical levels. The highest reached 159.019 during the move that began on September 24. Another reached 158.72 on October 12.

On each break, the buyers had their shot. Each time, they failed to sustain the momentum.

The downside rotations have varied, with swing lows near 157.524 and 157.425 helping to define the lower portion of the battle. Most of the price action has stayed inside the red box on the chart.

What the range teaches us

An important lesson in my book Attacking Currency Trends is to use technical tools to define risk and judge who has control.

When a recognizable midpoint and a longer-term moving average sit close together, they create a useful decision area. Sellers can lean against that area because it gives them a reference for where their trade starts to look wrong. Buyers know that getting above—and staying above—would strengthen their case.

The levels define the risk. The price action around them tells us whether that risk is being rewarded.

So far, the repeated failures above resistance tell us that buyers have struggled to turn a breakout into a trend. A move through a level is the first step. Follow-through, and the ability to hold above that level on a corrective move, provide stronger evidence that control is changing.

The hourly moving averages are the shorter-term barometer

Inside the range sit the 100- and 200-hour moving averages—the blue and green lines on the chart.

Admittedly, the price has moved above and below those averages, sometimes respecting them and sometimes passing through with little hesitation. That is what a market in a range can do. Buyers and sellers bob and weave, but neither side delivers the knockout punch.

That also provides an educational point: a moving-average break inside a range can shift the short-term bias without confirming a broader trend. Traders still need to pay attention to the next resistance or support level.

Currently, the price has moved above both hourly moving averages near 158.18, putting the shorter-term advantage with the buyers. However, the rally has so far stalled ahead of the 200-day moving average. Sellers still have a fighting chance.

What would put either fighter in control?

For buyers, the next job is to clear the 200-day moving average at 158.565 and hold above it. That would strengthen the bullish bias and bring the prior failed-break highs back into focus, including 158.72 and 159.019.

For sellers, holding below the 200-day moving average keeps their defense intact. A move back below the 50% midpoint at 158.419 would take some momentum away from the buyers and put the focus back on the hourly moving averages near 158.18.

A sustained break below those averages would shift the shorter-term advantage back toward sellers and reopen the door toward the lower swing areas.

For now, the buyers are landing the punches, and the sellers are closer to the ropes. But both sides have taken a beating during this extended range. The buyers are showing strength. They still need to get through resistance—and stay through it—to take firmer control of the fight.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: CIBC cuts gold forecasts but still sees $5,500 in 2028
item.description:
Gold bulls are getting a reminder that geopolitical turmoil doesn't always send bullion higher. Sometimes the inflation and interest-rate consequences overwhelm the safe-haven bid and sometimes the point of accumulating gold reserves is to use them when a shock -- like a war -- hits.

That's the challenge running through CIBC's latest precious metals outlook. The bank has sharply lowered its forecasts as higher energy prices, a stronger US dollar and a more hawkish Federal Reserve complicate the trade. But it still sees a substantial recovery over the next two years.

In its October report, CIBC cuts its 2027 average gold forecast to US$5,200 an ounce from $6,500. Its 2028 estimate falls to $5,500 from $6,000, while the fourth-quarter 2026 forecast drops to $4,500 from $6,500.

Those are sizeable revisions but still leave CIBC comfortably above the consensus estimates included in the report: $4,620 for 2027 and $4,451 for 2028.

“Despite this monetary policy headwind, we believe elevated geopolitical risk, fiscal concerns and continued diversification away from US Treasuries will underpin gold demand and support a recovery through 2027 and 2028," CIBC writes.

Gold is at $4147 more than 25% below its early-year peak near $5,600. Against that reference point, its 2028 average forecast implies a recovery of roughly 29%. The problem is getting there.

The report describes a market where the US-Iran conflict has supported demand for protection while simultaneously pushing oil prices and inflation expectations higher. That has strengthened the dollar and pushed the Fed toward tighter policy, undermining a non-yielding asset.

For traders, it's an awkward combination. More geopolitical risk can help gold, but another energy-price shock can also reinforce the very rate expectations holding it back.CIBC identifies a potential way out:

“In our view, gold could benefit if economic growth weakens or inflation moderates sufficiently to allow the Fed to pivot toward a more accommodative policy path than is currently reflected in market expectations or the FOMC’s projections.”

That puts the inflation and growth data squarely in focus. A sustained recovery would be easier with some relief from real yields and the dollar.

There is also a significant investment-demand assumption behind the bullish forecasts. CIBC projects gold ETF demand of 1,000 tonnes in each of 2027 and 2028, compared with just 35 tonnes in 2026. It also expects central-bank purchases to reach 1,000 tonnes annually in those two years.

Silver gets an even bigger near-term downgrade. CIBC cuts its 2027 forecast to $85 an ounce from $120, although that remains well above the report's $66 consensus estimate.

Copper goes the other way, with CIBC raising its forecast to $6.50 a pound for the fourth quarter and both 2027 and 2028.

“Demand growth is increasingly driven by grid modernization, electrification, renewable energy and digital infrastructure while new supply remains constrained by long development timelines, capital inflation and operating disruptions.”

The distinction is useful. Copper's upgraded outlook rests on physical demand and constrained supply. Gold's recovery depends more heavily on investment flows and how the monetary-policy backdrop evolves.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stocks close lower across the board as bond yields climb
item.description:
As London/European traders head home, the major European stock indices are closing lower across the board. Italy and Spain led the declines, but there was little separation, with all five major markets falling more than 1%. Not a good day. 

The closing snapshot showed:

  • Germany’s DAX: 25,319.78, down 302.84 points or 1.18%.

  • France’s CAC: 7,868.06, down 88.63 points or 1.11%.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: 10,764.70, down 117.21 points or 1.08%.

  • Spain’s Ibex: 19,039.30, down 287.00 points or 1.49%.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: 49,086.28, down 770.89 points or 1.55%.

After last week’s gains, sellers had their say to start the new trading week.

European Bond yields move higher with France leading the way. 

European benchmark 10-year yields moved higher, with France leading the way:

  • Germany: 3.456%, up 3.6 basis points.

  • France: 4.940%, up 8.6 basis points.

  • UK: 5.443%, up 3.9 basis points.

  • Spain: 4.080%, up 3.0 basis points.

  • Italy: 4.582%, up 5.0 basis points.

The French move stands out. Its yield rose 5 basis points more than Germany’s, widening the spread between the two countries. France's 10 year yield is near the highest level going back to May 2002.

There is a key budget vote in France set for tomorrow. The National Assembly is scheduled to hold a formal vote on the first part of the budget bill, covering government revenues, after parliamentary questions. The full budget vote is scheduled for November 17.

Tomorrow's vote matters as a test of the government's ability to deliver fiscal consolidation. A smooth passage would offer some relief and give the euro a boost, while a rejection or major concessions that weaken the deficit-reduction plan could put further pressure on French bonds and the euro.

US stocks rebound, led by the Nasdaq

As European traders head home, US stocks are trading higher, with the Nasdaq indices leading the way. The Dow is near unchanged, highlighting the stronger buying in technology shares.
